Adequate minimum wage protection is essential to **guarantee adequate working and living conditions, as well as to build fair and resilient economies and societies** as set out by Principle 6 of the European Pillar of Social Rights.

## Why this matters
*   Better working and living conditions, including through adequate minimum wages,**benefit both workers and businesses**in the Union   
*   Adequate minimum wages contribute to ensuring**fair competition**, stimulating **productivity improvements** and promoting **economic and social progress**   
*   They also contribute to improving the situation of other**low-wage earners**as minimum wage increases can also **boost low wages that are close to the minimum wage**
The role of minimum wages becomes even more important during economic downturns or periods of high inflation, as they can support low-paid workers and domestic demand. Ensuring a **decent living for workers and reducing in-work poverty is important for sustainable and inclusive economic growth**.

## Directive on adequate minimum wages in the EU
Minimum wage protection **exists in all EU countries** and is ensured either by legislative provisions (“statutory minimum wages”) and/or by collective agreements. However, the impact assessment published in October 2020 showed that, **in the majority of EU countries, workers were affected by low adequacy and/or gaps in the coverage of minimum wage protection**.
In light of this, based on theproposal of the European Commission, the**Directive on adequate minimum wages in the EU** was adopted by the European Parliament and the Council on 19 October 2022.EU countries were required to transpose the Directive into national law by 15 November 2024.
The Directive establishes a**framework**to:
*   improve the **adequacy of statutory minimum wages**  
*   promote **collective bargaining on wages**  
*   increase the**access of workers to minimum wage protection**

## Directive on adequate minimum wages in the EU
### All EU countries are asked to:
*   take measures to facilitate the exercise of the right of **collective bargaining on wage setting** and (further) increase the coverage of collective bargaining. Moreover, whenever collective bargaining coverage is below 80%, EU countries have to provide for a framework of enabling conditions and an action plan to promote collective bargaining   
*   enhance **enforcement and monitoring**, notably by developing effective data collection tools on minimum wage coverage and adequacy and by ensuring access for workers to effective and impartial dispute resolution and a right to redress

## Directive on adequate minimum wages in the EU
### EU countries with statutory minimum wages are additionally asked to:
*   put in place a procedural**framework for the setting and updating of statutory minimum wages**,including the use of clear criteria and of indicative reference values to guide the assessment of adequacy, as well as regular and timely updates of statutory minimum wages and the establishment of consultative bodies to advise the competent authorities   
*   ensure that **minimum wage variations and deductions** respect the principles of non-discrimination and proportionality   
*   ensure the **effective involvement of social partners**in statutory minimum wage setting and updating
The Directive also introduces**biannual reporting**by all EU countries on its minimum wage protection data to the Commission. The Commission is required to analyse these data, as well as the action plans to promote collective bargaining, and report in this regard to the European Parliament and the Council.
The firstmonitoring report from the Commission, together with its accompanyingstaff working document, was published in July 2026.
Subsidiarity principle and legal basis
The Directive fully respects thesubsidiarity principle: it foresees a**framework of minimum standards**, respecting and reflecting EU countries' competences and social partners' autonomy and contractual freedom in the field of wages. It does not oblige EU countries relying on collective agreements to introduce statutory minimum wages, nor does it establish the level of pay or set a harmonised minimum wage.
The Directive is based onArticle 153(1) (b) of theTreaty on the Functioning of the EU(TFEU) on working conditions.

## 6. Relationship and Structure Analysis
### 6.1. Relationship Between Minimum and Average Wages: Convergence, Concentration, Spillover Effects
Simultaneous convergence between minimum and average wages also generates structural wage compression at the lower end of the earnings distribution. This may reduce in-work poverty while also contributing to greater social cohesion; however, it can flatten wage hierarchies, providing little reward for skills and experience in some sectors. This phenomenon has led to debate about potential disincentives for upskilling and internal promotion in France and Portugal, where the Kaitz index is already high.
Another major dimension is sectoral concentration. The proportion of workers earning at or near the minimum wage varies greatly between countries and sectors. Where the share of minimum wage workers is high, changes in statutory wage floors can have larger aggregate effects on average wage statistics, especially in low-wage sectors. In countries with strong collective bargaining, such as Austria and Denmark, sectoral agreements often set entry wages above statutory-equivalent floors and therefore reduce the direct statistical link between minimum and average wages (Garnero, 2021; Eurofound, 2024).
Furthermore, Figure 5 presents the share of employees earnings less than 105% of the minimum wage, in October 2022, for several countries of interest.
Convergence processes may also reflect broader political–economic models. In coordinated market economies, such as Germany and the Netherlands, the relationship between minimum and average wages tends to be mediated by collective institutions, preserving wage differentiation. In liberal or state-driven models such as Hungary and Greece, the relationship is more directly shaped by state intervention. As a result, these systems often exhibit stronger mechanical wage convergence but, in some cases, weaker alignment with productivity.
Over the last decade, political initiatives, institutional reforms, and inflationary dynamics have tightened the relationship between minimum and average wages in the EU. Convergence has led to wage compression, reducing earnings inequality and improving social adequacy, although with potential trade-offs for skill incentives and productivity alignment. Going forward, this relationship will depend on how Member States balance statutory wage-setting mechanisms, collective bargaining coverage, and productivity growth in an environment characterised by persistent inflation and low economic growth.

## 6. Relationship and Structure Analysis
### 6.1. Relationship Between Minimum and Average Wages: Convergence, Concentration, Spillover Effects
To clarify the comparative framework of the analysis, Table 4 summarises the main national cases examined in the present article. The table provides an overview of wage-setting mechanisms, key wage developments, employment outcomes, implications for convergence, and the main policy lessons emerging from the comparison. It complements the preceding discussion by highlighting the similarities and differences across countries that are the most relevant for understanding the effects of the minimum wage policies.
**Table 4.** Comparative overview of selected national wage-setting systems and outcomes.

## 6. Relationship and Structure Analysis
### 6.2. Impact on Inequality
The way minimum and average wages relate to each other has direct implications for earnings inequality inside EU Member States. Many empirical studies and institutional reports note that higher minimum wages, when accompanied by limited top wage dispersion, can significantly reduce wage inequality (OECD, 2022; Eurofound, 2021). By reducing the incidence of extremely low pay, they compress wage gaps between the bottom and the middle of the wage distribution, which is where statutory wage floors have their greatest impact.
Evidence from countries that raised minimum wages rapidly, including Lithuania, Poland, and Romania, points to lower-tail wage compression and a reduction in the incidence of very low pay. The magnitude of these effects varies by country and depends on enforcement, tax–benefit systems, and the broader wage distribution. For this reason, this analysis avoids attributing precise changes in the Gini coefficient or the 90/10 wage ratio to minimum wage policy unless the underlying study directly estimates them.
In Western European countries, where wage inequality is generally more stable and minimum wages do not play a dominant role because of high collective bargaining coverage, the effects of minimum wages on reducing inequality are still present but more modest. For example, in Germany, recent studies on the introduction of a statutory minimum wage in 2015 have found evidence of reductions in lower tail wage dispersion, with stronger impacts on women, part-time workers, and employees in the eastern regions (Dustmann et al., 2022). However, the effects on overall income inequality were constrained by rising top-end wages.
Conversely, in countries where minimum wages remained low or stagnant relative to median earnings—such as Czechia or Slovakia—the reduction in inequality has been more limited. Moreover, in Southern European countries like Italy, where no statutory minimum wage exists, and Spain, where rapid increases only began in 2019, the inequality-reducing impact has been more recent and more sector-specific (Hijzen et al., 2023).

## 6. Relationship and Structure Analysis
### 6.2. Impact on Inequality
The institutional environment is important in determining whether the inequality effects of minimum wages are amplified or mitigated. Countries with high collective bargaining coverage and progressive taxation systems are more likely to see minimum wage policies translate into broader income equalisation (Garnero, 2021). Conversely, in countries with weak enforcement mechanisms or large informal economies, nominal increases in minimum wages often do not reach a significant proportion of low-wage earners, thereby limiting redistributive impact.
Women, young workers, and part-time employees are likely to benefit disproportionately from stronger minimum wage protection because they are overrepresented in low-paid sectors such as hospitality, retail, care, and personal services. The gender equality effect is therefore plausible, but its size depends on sectoral coverage, enforcement, and whether wage increases are accompanied by broader collective bargaining and working-time protections (Eurofound, 2022; European Commission, 2022).
Wage compression without upward mobility may occur if middle and upper-tier wages do not increase along with the minimum, while minimum wages are also rising. In addition, in the absence of parallel training, productivity, and public service investments, the impact of reducing poverty through minimum wages would be short-lived or would instead be shifted into higher costs of living.
Overall, the minimum wage strengthening mechanisms across the EU have led to a moderate decrease in wage and earnings inequality, particularly in low- and middle-income countries that previously exhibited higher levels of wage dispersion. The magnitude of this impact depends on institutional structures and complementary policies, as well as the extent to which wage increases are sustained and effectively enforced. As the EU advances towards greater wage convergence, ensuring that equity gains become structurally embedded, rather than remaining temporary or being reversed by economic cycles or eroded inflation, will remain a major challenge.
Finally, in Figure 6 below is presented the proportion of low-wage earners in EU countries for the year 2022.
**Figure 6.** Proportion of low-wage earners in EU countries, 2022. Source: Eurostat, Earnings statistics; Structure of Earnings Survey (earn_ses_pub1s).

## 6. Relationship and Structure Analysis
### 6.3. Impact on Unemployment and Working Hours
Raising the minimum wage has often been followed by fears of negative effects on employment and working hours, especially for low-skilled workers, young people, and small businesses. However, empirical evidence from across the European Union since 2015 shows that such effects are highly context-dependent and generally smaller than predicted by traditional economic models, particularly when increases are implemented gradually, carefully targeted, and accompanied by complementary institutional support measures.
In terms of unemployment, most post-2019 studies do not find a strong or systematic increase in joblessness following moderate or even substantial minimum wage hikes. For Germany, research on the 2015 reform and subsequent adjustments finds no large aggregate unemployment effect, although marginal employment and firm-level reallocation did occur (Caliendo et al., 2018; Bossler & Gerner, 2020; Dustmann et al., 2022; Holtemöller & Pohle, 2020). Evidence from Lithuania and other Central and Eastern European countries similarly suggests that rapid wage growth can coexist with low unemployment when labour demand is strong.
In Spain, the 2019 increase was large and therefore particularly relevant for assessing potential risks. The evidence indicates limited aggregate employment effects but points to greater vulnerability among temporary, young, agricultural, and low-productivity workers. This means that minimum wage policy should be monitored not only through total employment, but also across sectors, age groups, contract types, and regions (Banco de España, 2020; Hijzen et al., 2023).
Although total unemployment does not increase, there is some evidence to suggest that firms adjust on the intensive margin-meaning working hours, not headcount. Firms facing higher wage floors in France and Belgium have at times responded by limiting overtime, shifting workers to part-time contracts, or simply by reducing weekly working hours, especially in low-margin industries (INSEE, 2023; ETUI, 2023). Surveys in Greece have indicated reduced average working hours per week among workers in the accommodation and food service sectors after recent minimum wage increases. This may reflect cost-control strategies adopted by small firms (INE GSEE, 2023).

# The share of minimum wage earners across Europe – from highest to lowest
## The share of workers earning the minimum wage differs sharply across Europe. The European Commission is calling for fair and adequate pay to guarantee a decent standard of living.
Around 13 million workers across 21 EU countries earn the minimum wage or less, according to Eurostat. The European Commission actively supports fair and adequate minimum wages to ensure a decent standard of living for all workers.

But which countries have the highest share of minimum wage earners — and where do those workers enjoy the greatest purchasing power?
Eurostat estimates that in 2022 the share of employees earning less than 105% of the minimum wage ranged from 2.6% in Czechia to 13.0% in Bulgaria.
Because the earnings concept in the minimum wage definition and in the earnings survey differ, Eurostat sets the cut-off at 105% of the minimum wage (a 5% mark-up) to approximate the share of minimum-wage earners.

# The share of minimum wage earners across Europe – from highest to lowest
## The share of workers earning the minimum wage differs sharply across Europe. The European Commission is calling for fair and adequate pay to guarantee a decent standard of living.
### **At least one in ten workers in seven EU countries**
The share of workers earning the minimum wage or less is 10% or higher in seven EU countries. Alongside the top-ranked Bulgaria, these include France (12.7%), Slovenia (12.6%), Romania (10.5%), Greece (10.2%), Poland (10.1%) and Hungary (10%).
At the other end of the scale, Czechia (2.6%), Portugal (3.1%), Estonia (3.3%), the Netherlands (3.5%), Malta (3.5%) and Spain (3.6%) record the lowest proportions — all below 4%.
Among Europe’s largest economies, France has the highest share of minimum wage earners (12.7%), compared with 8% in Germany, 6.5% in the UK and 3.6% in Spain.
According to the OECD, collective bargaining plays a key role in shaping these figures.
“Countries with stronger labour institutions and collective agreements tend to have fewer cases of workers being paid below the minimum wage,” Dr Stefano Filauro from Sapienza University of Rome told _Euronews Business_.
He added that advanced economies with more high-skilled, high-paid sectors tend to have fewer low-wage workers, while weak labour inspections and limited penalties for non-compliance often allow underpayment to persist.
There is no statutory minimum wage in Italy, Austria, Sweden, Denmark or Finland.

# The share of minimum wage earners across Europe – from highest to lowest
## Turkey stands out as a major outlier
Turkey remains an outlier, with a much larger share of workers on or below the minimum wage. The Confederation of Progressive Trade Unions of Turkey (DİSK) reports that 37.5% of Turkish workers earned the minimum wage or less in 2022.
The data for the UK and Turkey come from national sources rather than Eurostat, so they are not directly comparable with EU figures.
In the mid-2010s, Eurostat estimated that around 43% of Turkish workers earned the minimum wage, with similar figures reported in 2020.
“In Turkey, the minimum wage has long ceased to be a floor and has become the average wage,” DİSK said in a statement in October 2025. “With trade union rights under constant pressure, millions of workers are forced to survive on or around the minimum wage.”

# The share of minimum wage earners across Europe – from highest to lowest
## **How many people earn the minimum wage?**
The exact number of minimum wage earners is difficult to determine and often varies between data sources, according to the OECD. Eurostat provides its own estimates, but small firms are frequently excluded, meaning the true number is likely higher.
Using 2022 data, France had the highest number of minimum wage earners in 2024 — about 3.5 million people — followed by Germany with 3.2 million.
Across 21 EU countries, the total stood at 12.8 million. The UK had around 1.9 million, while Turkey recorded 11.2 million — just 1.6 million fewer than the combined total of those 21 EU states.

# The share of minimum wage earners across Europe – from highest to lowest
## Minimum wage and income inequality
“The impact of minimum wages on income inequality in the EU” report published by the Commission’s Joint Research Centre pointed out that minimum wage policies have an impact on national income distributions across EU countries and thus, they also have the potential to influence the distribution of income across the overall EU population.
The purchasing power of the minimum wage varies widely across Europe. The five countries with the highest minimum wages in purchasing power standards (PPS) are Luxembourg (2,035), Germany (1,989), the Netherlands (1,937), Belgium (1,812), and Ireland (1,653).
The lowest figures are recorded in Estonia (886), Latvia (905), Bulgaria (922), Czechia (936) and Slovakia (963).
EU candidate countries North Macedonia (1,069), Turkey (1,062), and Montenegro (1,058) have higher minimum wages in PPS than several EU member states.
In October 2022, the European Commission adopted a directive on adequate minimum wages in the EU, aiming to ensure that workers’ earnings are sufficient to provide a decent standard of living across the Union.

# The share of minimum wage earners across Europe – from highest to lowest
## The share of workers earning the minimum wage differs sharply across Europe. The European Commission is calling for fair and adequate pay to guarantee a decent standard of living.
Around 13 million workers across 21 EU countries earn the minimum wage or less, according to Eurostat. The European Commission actively supports fair and adequate minimum wages to ensure a decent standard of living for all workers.
ADVERTISEMENT
ADVERTISEMENT
But which countries have the highest share of minimum wage earners — and where do those workers enjoy the greatest purchasing power?
Eurostat estimates that in 2022 the share of employees earning less than 105% of the minimum wage ranged from 2.6% in Czechia to 13.0% in Bulgaria.
Because the earnings concept in the minimum wage definition and in the earnings survey differ, Eurostat sets the cut-off at 105% of the minimum wage (a 5% mark-up) to approximate the share of minimum-wage earners.

# The share of minimum wage earners across Europe – from highest to lowest
## The share of workers earning the minimum wage differs sharply across Europe. The European Commission is calling for fair and adequate pay to guarantee a decent standard of living.
### **At least one in ten workers in seven EU countries**
The share of workers earning the minimum wage or less is 10% or higher in seven EU countries. Alongside the top-ranked Bulgaria, these include France (12.7%), Slovenia (12.6%), Romania (10.5%), Greece (10.2%), Poland (10.1%) and Hungary (10%).
At the other end of the scale, Czechia (2.6%), Portugal (3.1%), Estonia (3.3%), the Netherlands (3.5%), Malta (3.5%) and Spain (3.6%) record the lowest proportions — all below 4%.
Among Europe’s largest economies, France has the highest share of minimum wage earners (12.7%), compared with 8% in Germany, 6.5% in the UK and 3.6% in Spain.
According to the OECD, collective bargaining plays a key role in shaping these figures.
“Countries with stronger labour institutions and collective agreements tend to have fewer cases of workers being paid below the minimum wage,” Dr Stefano Filauro from Sapienza University of Rome told _Euronews Business_.
He added that advanced economies with more high-skilled, high-paid sectors tend to have fewer low-wage workers, while weak labour inspections and limited penalties for non-compliance often allow underpayment to persist.
There is no statutory minimum wage in Italy, Austria, Sweden, Denmark or Finland.

# The share of minimum wage earners across Europe – from highest to lowest
## Turkey stands out as a major outlier
Turkey remains an outlier, with a much larger share of workers on or below the minimum wage. The Confederation of Progressive Trade Unions of Turkey (DİSK) reports that 37.5% of Turkish workers earned the minimum wage or less in 2022.
The data for the UK and Turkey come from national sources rather than Eurostat, so they are not directly comparable with EU figures.
In the mid-2010s, Eurostat estimated that around 43% of Turkish workers earned the minimum wage, with similar figures reported in 2020.
“In Turkey, the minimum wage has long ceased to be a floor and has become the average wage,” DİSK said in a statement in October 2025. “With trade union rights under constant pressure, millions of workers are forced to survive on or around the minimum wage.”

# The share of minimum wage earners across Europe – from highest to lowest
## **How many people earn the minimum wage?**
The exact number of minimum wage earners is difficult to determine and often varies between data sources, according to the OECD. Eurostat provides its own estimates, but small firms are frequently excluded, meaning the true number is likely higher.
Using 2022 data, France had the highest number of minimum wage earners in 2024 — about 3.5 million people — followed by Germany with 3.2 million.
Across 21 EU countries, the total stood at 12.8 million. The UK had around 1.9 million, while Turkey recorded 11.2 million — just 1.6 million fewer than the combined total of those 21 EU states.

# The share of minimum wage earners across Europe – from highest to lowest
## Minimum wage and income inequality
“The impact of minimum wages on income inequality in the EU” report published by the Commission’s Joint Research Centre pointed out that minimum wage policies have an impact on national income distributions across EU countries and thus, they also have the potential to influence the distribution of income across the overall EU population.
The purchasing power of the minimum wage varies widely across Europe. The five countries with the highest minimum wages in purchasing power standards (PPS) are Luxembourg (2,035), Germany (1,989), the Netherlands (1,937), Belgium (1,812), and Ireland (1,653).
The lowest figures are recorded in Estonia (886), Latvia (905), Bulgaria (922), Czechia (936) and Slovakia (963).
EU candidate countries North Macedonia (1,069), Turkey (1,062), and Montenegro (1,058) have higher minimum wages in PPS than several EU member states.
In October 2022, the European Commission adopted a directive on adequate minimum wages in the EU, aiming to ensure that workers’ earnings are sufficient to provide a decent standard of living across the Union.

## 6. Relationship and Structure Analysis
### 6.1. Relationship Between Minimum and Average Wages: Convergence, Concentration, Spillover Effects
Simultaneous convergence between minimum and average wages also generates structural wage compression at the lower end of the earnings distribution. This may reduce in-work poverty while also contributing to greater social cohesion; however, it can flatten wage hierarchies, providing little reward for skills and experience in some sectors. This phenomenon has led to debate about potential disincentives for upskilling and internal promotion in France and Portugal, where the Kaitz index is already high.
Another major dimension is sectoral concentration. The proportion of workers earning at or near the minimum wage varies greatly between countries and sectors. Where the share of minimum wage workers is high, changes in statutory wage floors can have larger aggregate effects on average wage statistics, especially in low-wage sectors. In countries with strong collective bargaining, such as Austria and Denmark, sectoral agreements often set entry wages above statutory-equivalent floors and therefore reduce the direct statistical link between minimum and average wages (Garnero, 2021; Eurofound, 2024).
Furthermore, Figure 5 presents the share of employees earnings less than 105% of the minimum wage, in October 2022, for several countries of interest.
Convergence processes may also reflect broader political–economic models. In coordinated market economies, such as Germany and the Netherlands, the relationship between minimum and average wages tends to be mediated by collective institutions, preserving wage differentiation. In liberal or state-driven models such as Hungary and Greece, the relationship is more directly shaped by state intervention. As a result, these systems often exhibit stronger mechanical wage convergence but, in some cases, weaker alignment with productivity.
Over the last decade, political initiatives, institutional reforms, and inflationary dynamics have tightened the relationship between minimum and average wages in the EU. Convergence has led to wage compression, reducing earnings inequality and improving social adequacy, although with potential trade-offs for skill incentives and productivity alignment. Going forward, this relationship will depend on how Member States balance statutory wage-setting mechanisms, collective bargaining coverage, and productivity growth in an environment characterised by persistent inflation and low economic growth.

## 6. Relationship and Structure Analysis
### 6.2. Impact on Inequality
The way minimum and average wages relate to each other has direct implications for earnings inequality inside EU Member States. Many empirical studies and institutional reports note that higher minimum wages, when accompanied by limited top wage dispersion, can significantly reduce wage inequality (OECD, 2022; Eurofound, 2021). By reducing the incidence of extremely low pay, they compress wage gaps between the bottom and the middle of the wage distribution, which is where statutory wage floors have their greatest impact.
Evidence from countries that raised minimum wages rapidly, including Lithuania, Poland, and Romania, points to lower-tail wage compression and a reduction in the incidence of very low pay. The magnitude of these effects varies by country and depends on enforcement, tax–benefit systems, and the broader wage distribution. For this reason, this analysis avoids attributing precise changes in the Gini coefficient or the 90/10 wage ratio to minimum wage policy unless the underlying study directly estimates them.
In Western European countries, where wage inequality is generally more stable and minimum wages do not play a dominant role because of high collective bargaining coverage, the effects of minimum wages on reducing inequality are still present but more modest. For example, in Germany, recent studies on the introduction of a statutory minimum wage in 2015 have found evidence of reductions in lower tail wage dispersion, with stronger impacts on women, part-time workers, and employees in the eastern regions (Dustmann et al., 2022). However, the effects on overall income inequality were constrained by rising top-end wages.
Conversely, in countries where minimum wages remained low or stagnant relative to median earnings—such as Czechia or Slovakia—the reduction in inequality has been more limited. Moreover, in Southern European countries like Italy, where no statutory minimum wage exists, and Spain, where rapid increases only began in 2019, the inequality-reducing impact has been more recent and more sector-specific (Hijzen et al., 2023).

## 6. Relationship and Structure Analysis
### 6.2. Impact on Inequality
The institutional environment is important in determining whether the inequality effects of minimum wages are amplified or mitigated. Countries with high collective bargaining coverage and progressive taxation systems are more likely to see minimum wage policies translate into broader income equalisation (Garnero, 2021). Conversely, in countries with weak enforcement mechanisms or large informal economies, nominal increases in minimum wages often do not reach a significant proportion of low-wage earners, thereby limiting redistributive impact.
Women, young workers, and part-time employees are likely to benefit disproportionately from stronger minimum wage protection because they are overrepresented in low-paid sectors such as hospitality, retail, care, and personal services. The gender equality effect is therefore plausible, but its size depends on sectoral coverage, enforcement, and whether wage increases are accompanied by broader collective bargaining and working-time protections (Eurofound, 2022; European Commission, 2022).
Wage compression without upward mobility may occur if middle and upper-tier wages do not increase along with the minimum, while minimum wages are also rising. In addition, in the absence of parallel training, productivity, and public service investments, the impact of reducing poverty through minimum wages would be short-lived or would instead be shifted into higher costs of living.
Overall, the minimum wage strengthening mechanisms across the EU have led to a moderate decrease in wage and earnings inequality, particularly in low- and middle-income countries that previously exhibited higher levels of wage dispersion. The magnitude of this impact depends on institutional structures and complementary policies, as well as the extent to which wage increases are sustained and effectively enforced. As the EU advances towards greater wage convergence, ensuring that equity gains become structurally embedded, rather than remaining temporary or being reversed by economic cycles or eroded inflation, will remain a major challenge.

## 6. Relationship and Structure Analysis
### 6.3. Impact on Unemployment and Working Hours
Raising the minimum wage has often been followed by fears of negative effects on employment and working hours, especially for low-skilled workers, young people, and small businesses. However, empirical evidence from across the European Union since 2015 shows that such effects are highly context-dependent and generally smaller than predicted by traditional economic models, particularly when increases are implemented gradually, carefully targeted, and accompanied by complementary institutional support measures.
In terms of unemployment, most post-2019 studies do not find a strong or systematic increase in joblessness following moderate or even substantial minimum wage hikes. For Germany, research on the 2015 reform and subsequent adjustments finds no large aggregate unemployment effect, although marginal employment and firm-level reallocation did occur (Caliendo et al., 2018; Bossler & Gerner, 2020; Dustmann et al., 2022; Holtemöller & Pohle, 2020). Evidence from Lithuania and other Central and Eastern European countries similarly suggests that rapid wage growth can coexist with low unemployment when labour demand is strong.
In Spain, the 2019 increase was large and therefore particularly relevant for assessing potential risks. The evidence indicates limited aggregate employment effects but points to greater vulnerability among temporary, young, agricultural, and low-productivity workers. This means that minimum wage policy should be monitored not only through total employment, but also across sectors, age groups, contract types, and regions (Banco de España, 2020; Hijzen et al., 2023).
Although total unemployment does not increase, there is some evidence to suggest that firms adjust on the intensive margin-meaning working hours, not headcount. Firms facing higher wage floors in France and Belgium have at times responded by limiting overtime, shifting workers to part-time contracts, or simply by reducing weekly working hours, especially in low-margin industries (INSEE, 2023; ETUI, 2023). Surveys in Greece have indicated reduced average working hours per week among workers in the accommodation and food service sectors after recent minimum wage increases. This may reflect cost-control strategies adopted by small firms (INE GSEE, 2023).

## Why this matters
*   Better working and living conditions, including through adequate minimum wages,**benefit both workers and businesses**in the Union   
*   Adequate minimum wages contribute to ensuring**fair competition**, stimulating **productivity improvements** and promoting **economic and social progress**   
*   They also contribute to improving the situation of other**low-wage earners**as minimum wage increases can also **boost low wages that are close to the minimum wage**
The role of minimum wages becomes even more important during economic downturns or periods of high inflation, as they can support low-paid workers and domestic demand. Ensuring a **decent living for workers and reducing in-work poverty is important for sustainable and inclusive economic growth**.
texts.2:
## Directive on adequate minimum wages in the EU
Minimum wage protection **exists in all EU countries** and is ensured either by legislative provisions (“statutory minimum wages”) and/or by collective agreements. However, the impact assessment published in October 2020 showed that, **in the majority of EU countries, workers were affected by low adequacy and/or gaps in the coverage of minimum wage protection**.
In light of this, based on theproposal of the European Commission, the**Directive on adequate minimum wages in the EU** was adopted by the European Parliament and the Council on 19 October 2022.EU countries were required to transpose the Directive into national law by 15 November 2024.
The Directive establishes a**framework**to:
*   improve the **adequacy of statutory minimum wages**  
*   promote **collective bargaining on wages**  
*   increase the**access of workers to minimum wage protection**
texts.3:
## Directive on adequate minimum wages in the EU
### All EU countries are asked to:
*   take measures to facilitate the exercise of the right of **collective bargaining on wage setting** and (further) increase the coverage of collective bargaining. Moreover, whenever collective bargaining coverage is below 80%, EU countries have to provide for a framework of enabling conditions and an action plan to promote collective bargaining   
*   enhance **enforcement and monitoring**, notably by developing effective data collection tools on minimum wage coverage and adequacy and by ensuring access for workers to effective and impartial dispute resolution and a right to redress
texts.4:
## Directive on adequate minimum wages in the EU
### EU countries with statutory minimum wages are additionally asked to:
*   put in place a procedural**framework for the setting and updating of statutory minimum wages**,including the use of clear criteria and of indicative reference values to guide the assessment of adequacy, as well as regular and timely updates of statutory minimum wages and the establishment of consultative bodies to advise the competent authorities   
*   ensure that **minimum wage variations and deductions** respect the principles of non-discrimination and proportionality   
*   ensure the **effective involvement of social partners**in statutory minimum wage setting and updating
The Directive also introduces**biannual reporting**by all EU countries on its minimum wage protection data to the Commission. The Commission is required to analyse these data, as well as the action plans to promote collective bargaining, and report in this regard to the European Parliament and the Council.
The firstmonitoring report from the Commission, together with its accompanyingstaff working document, was published in July 2026.
Subsidiarity principle and legal basis
The Directive fully respects thesubsidiarity principle: it foresees a**framework of minimum standards**, respecting and reflecting EU countries' competences and social partners' autonomy and contractual freedom in the field of wages. It does not oblige EU countries relying on collective agreements to introduce statutory minimum wages, nor does it establish the level of pay or set a harmonised minimum wage.
The Directive is based onArticle 153(1) (b) of theTreaty on the Functioning of the EU(TFEU) on working conditions.

## The share of workers earning the minimum wage differs sharply across Europe. The European Commission is calling for fair and adequate pay to guarantee a decent standard of living.
### **At least one in ten workers in seven EU countries**
The share of workers earning the minimum wage or less is 10% or higher in seven EU countries. Alongside the top-ranked Bulgaria, these include France (12.7%), Slovenia (12.6%), Romania (10.5%), Greece (10.2%), Poland (10.1%) and Hungary (10%).
At the other end of the scale, Czechia (2.6%), Portugal (3.1%), Estonia (3.3%), the Netherlands (3.5%), Malta (3.5%) and Spain (3.6%) record the lowest proportions — all below 4%.
Among Europe’s largest economies, France has the highest share of minimum wage earners (12.7%), compared with 8% in Germany, 6.5% in the UK and 3.6% in Spain.
According to the OECD, collective bargaining plays a key role in shaping these figures.
“Countries with stronger labour institutions and collective agreements tend to have fewer cases of workers being paid below the minimum wage,” Dr Stefano Filauro from Sapienza University of Rome told _Euronews Business_.
He added that advanced economies with more high-skilled, high-paid sectors tend to have fewer low-wage workers, while weak labour inspections and limited penalties for non-compliance often allow underpayment to persist.
There is no statutory minimum wage in Italy, Austria, Sweden, Denmark or Finland.

# The share of minimum wage earners across Europe – from highest to lowest
## Turkey stands out as a major outlier
Turkey remains an outlier, with a much larger share of workers on or below the minimum wage. The Confederation of Progressive Trade Unions of Turkey (DİSK) reports that 37.5% of Turkish workers earned the minimum wage or less in 2022.
The data for the UK and Turkey come from national sources rather than Eurostat, so they are not directly comparable with EU figures.
In the mid-2010s, Eurostat estimated that around 43% of Turkish workers earned the minimum wage, with similar figures reported in 2020.
“In Turkey, the minimum wage has long ceased to be a floor and has become the average wage,” DİSK said in a statement in October 2025. “With trade union rights under constant pressure, millions of workers are forced to survive on or around the minimum wage.”

# The share of minimum wage earners across Europe – from highest to lowest
## **How many people earn the minimum wage?**
The exact number of minimum wage earners is difficult to determine and often varies between data sources, according to the OECD. Eurostat provides its own estimates, but small firms are frequently excluded, meaning the true number is likely higher.
Using 2022 data, France had the highest number of minimum wage earners in 2024 — about 3.5 million people — followed by Germany with 3.2 million.
Across 21 EU countries, the total stood at 12.8 million. The UK had around 1.9 million, while Turkey recorded 11.2 million — just 1.6 million fewer than the combined total of those 21 EU states.

## Minimum wage and income inequality
“The impact of minimum wages on income inequality in the EU” report published by the Commission’s Joint Research Centre pointed out that minimum wage policies have an impact on national income distributions across EU countries and thus, they also have the potential to influence the distribution of income across the overall EU population.
The purchasing power of the minimum wage varies widely across Europe. The five countries with the highest minimum wages in purchasing power standards (PPS) are Luxembourg (2,035), Germany (1,989), the Netherlands (1,937), Belgium (1,812), and Ireland (1,653).
The lowest figures are recorded in Estonia (886), Latvia (905), Bulgaria (922), Czechia (936) and Slovakia (963).
EU candidate countries North Macedonia (1,069), Turkey (1,062), and Montenegro (1,058) have higher minimum wages in PPS than several EU member states.
In October 2022, the European Commission adopted a directive on adequate minimum wages in the EU, aiming to ensure that workers’ earnings are sufficient to provide a decent standard of living across the Union.

## 6. Relationship and Structure Analysis
### 6.1. Relationship Between Minimum and Average Wages: Convergence, Concentration, Spillover Effects
Simultaneous convergence between minimum and average wages also generates structural wage compression at the lower end of the earnings distribution. This may reduce in-work poverty while also contributing to greater social cohesion; however, it can flatten wage hierarchies, providing little reward for skills and experience in some sectors. This phenomenon has led to debate about potential disincentives for upskilling and internal promotion in France and Portugal, where the Kaitz index is already high.
Another major dimension is sectoral concentration. The proportion of workers earning at or near the minimum wage varies greatly between countries and sectors. Where the share of minimum wage workers is high, changes in statutory wage floors can have larger aggregate effects on average wage statistics, especially in low-wage sectors. In countries with strong collective bargaining, such as Austria and Denmark, sectoral agreements often set entry wages above statutory-equivalent floors and therefore reduce the direct statistical link between minimum and average wages (Garnero, 2021; Eurofound, 2024).
Furthermore, Figure 5 presents the share of employees earnings less than 105% of the minimum wage, in October 2022, for several countries of interest.
Convergence processes may also reflect broader political–economic models. In coordinated market economies, such as Germany and the Netherlands, the relationship between minimum and average wages tends to be mediated by collective institutions, preserving wage differentiation. In liberal or state-driven models such as Hungary and Greece, the relationship is more directly shaped by state intervention. As a result, these systems often exhibit stronger mechanical wage convergence but, in some cases, weaker alignment with productivity.
Over the last decade, political initiatives, institutional reforms, and inflationary dynamics have tightened the relationship between minimum and average wages in the EU. Convergence has led to wage compression, reducing earnings inequality and improving social adequacy, although with potential trade-offs for skill incentives and productivity alignment. Going forward, this relationship will depend on how Member States balance statutory wage-setting mechanisms, collective bargaining coverage, and productivity growth in an environment characterised by persistent inflation and low economic growth.

## 6. Relationship and Structure Analysis
### 6.2. Impact on Inequality
The way minimum and average wages relate to each other has direct implications for earnings inequality inside EU Member States. Many empirical studies and institutional reports note that higher minimum wages, when accompanied by limited top wage dispersion, can significantly reduce wage inequality (OECD, 2022; Eurofound, 2021). By reducing the incidence of extremely low pay, they compress wage gaps between the bottom and the middle of the wage distribution, which is where statutory wage floors have their greatest impact.
Evidence from countries that raised minimum wages rapidly, including Lithuania, Poland, and Romania, points to lower-tail wage compression and a reduction in the incidence of very low pay. The magnitude of these effects varies by country and depends on enforcement, tax–benefit systems, and the broader wage distribution. For this reason, this analysis avoids attributing precise changes in the Gini coefficient or the 90/10 wage ratio to minimum wage policy unless the underlying study directly estimates them.
In Western European countries, where wage inequality is generally more stable and minimum wages do not play a dominant role because of high collective bargaining coverage, the effects of minimum wages on reducing inequality are still present but more modest. For example, in Germany, recent studies on the introduction of a statutory minimum wage in 2015 have found evidence of reductions in lower tail wage dispersion, with stronger impacts on women, part-time workers, and employees in the eastern regions (Dustmann et al., 2022). However, the effects on overall income inequality were constrained by rising top-end wages.
Conversely, in countries where minimum wages remained low or stagnant relative to median earnings—such as Czechia or Slovakia—the reduction in inequality has been more limited. Moreover, in Southern European countries like Italy, where no statutory minimum wage exists, and Spain, where rapid increases only began in 2019, the inequality-reducing impact has been more recent and more sector-specific (Hijzen et al., 2023).

## 6. Relationship and Structure Analysis
### 6.2. Impact on Inequality
The institutional environment is important in determining whether the inequality effects of minimum wages are amplified or mitigated. Countries with high collective bargaining coverage and progressive taxation systems are more likely to see minimum wage policies translate into broader income equalisation (Garnero, 2021). Conversely, in countries with weak enforcement mechanisms or large informal economies, nominal increases in minimum wages often do not reach a significant proportion of low-wage earners, thereby limiting redistributive impact.
Women, young workers, and part-time employees are likely to benefit disproportionately from stronger minimum wage protection because they are overrepresented in low-paid sectors such as hospitality, retail, care, and personal services. The gender equality effect is therefore plausible, but its size depends on sectoral coverage, enforcement, and whether wage increases are accompanied by broader collective bargaining and working-time protections (Eurofound, 2022; European Commission, 2022).
Wage compression without upward mobility may occur if middle and upper-tier wages do not increase along with the minimum, while minimum wages are also rising. In addition, in the absence of parallel training, productivity, and public service investments, the impact of reducing poverty through minimum wages would be short-lived or would instead be shifted into higher costs of living.
Overall, the minimum wage strengthening mechanisms across the EU have led to a moderate decrease in wage and earnings inequality, particularly in low- and middle-income countries that previously exhibited higher levels of wage dispersion. The magnitude of this impact depends on institutional structures and complementary policies, as well as the extent to which wage increases are sustained and effectively enforced. As the EU advances towards greater wage convergence, ensuring that equity gains become structurally embedded, rather than remaining temporary or being reversed by economic cycles or eroded inflation, will remain a major challenge.

## 6. Relationship and Structure Analysis
### 6.3. Impact on Unemployment and Working Hours
Raising the minimum wage has often been followed by fears of negative effects on employment and working hours, especially for low-skilled workers, young people, and small businesses. However, empirical evidence from across the European Union since 2015 shows that such effects are highly context-dependent and generally smaller than predicted by traditional economic models, particularly when increases are implemented gradually, carefully targeted, and accompanied by complementary institutional support measures.
In terms of unemployment, most post-2019 studies do not find a strong or systematic increase in joblessness following moderate or even substantial minimum wage hikes. For Germany, research on the 2015 reform and subsequent adjustments finds no large aggregate unemployment effect, although marginal employment and firm-level reallocation did occur (Caliendo et al., 2018; Bossler & Gerner, 2020; Dustmann et al., 2022; Holtemöller & Pohle, 2020). Evidence from Lithuania and other Central and Eastern European countries similarly suggests that rapid wage growth can coexist with low unemployment when labour demand is strong.
In Spain, the 2019 increase was large and therefore particularly relevant for assessing potential risks. The evidence indicates limited aggregate employment effects but points to greater vulnerability among temporary, young, agricultural, and low-productivity workers. This means that minimum wage policy should be monitored not only through total employment, but also across sectors, age groups, contract types, and regions (Banco de España, 2020; Hijzen et al., 2023).
Although total unemployment does not increase, there is some evidence to suggest that firms adjust on the intensive margin-meaning working hours, not headcount. Firms facing higher wage floors in France and Belgium have at times responded by limiting overtime, shifting workers to part-time contracts, or simply by reducing weekly working hours, especially in low-margin industries (INSEE, 2023; ETUI, 2023). Surveys in Greece have indicated reduced average working hours per week among workers in the accommodation and food service sectors after recent minimum wage increases. This may reflect cost-control strategies adopted by small firms (INE GSEE, 2023).

Adequate minimum wage protection is essential to **guarantee adequate working and living conditions, as well as to build fair and resilient economies and societies** as set out by Principle 6 of the European Pillar of Social Rights.

## Why this matters
*   Better working and living conditions, including through adequate minimum wages,**benefit both workers and businesses**in the Union   
*   Adequate minimum wages contribute to ensuring**fair competition**, stimulating **productivity improvements** and promoting **economic and social progress**   
*   They also contribute to improving the situation of other**low-wage earners**as minimum wage increases can also **boost low wages that are close to the minimum wage**
The role of minimum wages becomes even more important during economic downturns or periods of high inflation, as they can support low-paid workers and domestic demand. Ensuring a **decent living for workers and reducing in-work poverty is important for sustainable and inclusive economic growth**.

## Directive on adequate minimum wages in the EU
Minimum wage protection **exists in all EU countries** and is ensured either by legislative provisions (“statutory minimum wages”) and/or by collective agreements. However, the impact assessment published in October 2020 showed that, **in the majority of EU countries, workers were affected by low adequacy and/or gaps in the coverage of minimum wage protection**.
In light of this, based on theproposal of the European Commission, the**Directive on adequate minimum wages in the EU** was adopted by the European Parliament and the Council on 19 October 2022.EU countries were required to transpose the Directive into national law by 15 November 2024.
The Directive establishes a**framework**to:
*   improve the **adequacy of statutory minimum wages**  
*   promote **collective bargaining on wages**  
*   increase the**access of workers to minimum wage protection**

## Directive on adequate minimum wages in the EU
### All EU countries are asked to:
*   take measures to facilitate the exercise of the right of **collective bargaining on wage setting** and (further) increase the coverage of collective bargaining. Moreover, whenever collective bargaining coverage is below 80%, EU countries have to provide for a framework of enabling conditions and an action plan to promote collective bargaining   
*   enhance **enforcement and monitoring**, notably by developing effective data collection tools on minimum wage coverage and adequacy and by ensuring access for workers to effective and impartial dispute resolution and a right to redress

## Directive on adequate minimum wages in the EU
### EU countries with statutory minimum wages are additionally asked to:
*   put in place a procedural**framework for the setting and updating of statutory minimum wages**,including the use of clear criteria and of indicative reference values to guide the assessment of adequacy, as well as regular and timely updates of statutory minimum wages and the establishment of consultative bodies to advise the competent authorities   
*   ensure that **minimum wage variations and deductions** respect the principles of non-discrimination and proportionality   
*   ensure the **effective involvement of social partners**in statutory minimum wage setting and updating
The Directive also introduces**biannual reporting**by all EU countries on its minimum wage protection data to the Commission. The Commission is required to analyse these data, as well as the action plans to promote collective bargaining, and report in this regard to the European Parliament and the Council.
The firstmonitoring report from the Commission, together with its accompanyingstaff working document, was published in July 2026.
Subsidiarity principle and legal basis
The Directive fully respects thesubsidiarity principle: it foresees a**framework of minimum standards**, respecting and reflecting EU countries' competences and social partners' autonomy and contractual freedom in the field of wages. It does not oblige EU countries relying on collective agreements to introduce statutory minimum wages, nor does it establish the level of pay or set a harmonised minimum wage.
The Directive is based onArticle 153(1) (b) of theTreaty on the Functioning of the EU(TFEU) on working conditions.

## Union growth and decline
[edit]
In the mid-1950s, 36% of the United States labor force was unionized. At America's union peak in the 1950s, union membership was lower in the United States than in most comparable countries. By 1989, that figure had dropped to about 16%, the lowest percentage of any developed democracy, except France. Union membership for other developed democracies, in 1986/87 were:[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-wsj-3)
*   95% in Sweden and Denmark.  
*   85% in Finland  
*   Over 60% in Norway and Austria  
*   Over 50% in Australia, Ireland and the United Kingdom.  
*   Over 40% in Italy.  
*   Over 30% in West Germany.
In 1987, United States unionization was 37 points below the average of seventeen countries surveyed, down from 17 points below average in 1970.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-wsj-3) Between 1970 and 1987, union membership declined in only three other countries: Austria, by 3%, Japan, by 7%, and the Netherlands, by 4%. In the United States, union membership had declined by 14%.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-4)

## Union growth and decline
In 2008, 12.4% of U.S. wage and salary workers were union members. 36.8% of public sector workers were union members, but only 7.6% of workers in private sector industries were.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-5) The most unionized sectors of the economy have had the greatest decline in union membership. From 1953 to the late 1980s membership in construction fell from 84% to 22%, manufacturing from 42% to 25%, mining from 65% to 15%, and transportation from 80% to 37%.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-7)
From 1971 to the late 1980s, there was a 10% drop in union membership in the U.S. public sector and a 42% drop in union membership in the U.S. private sector.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-8) For comparison, there was no drop in union membership in the private sector in Sweden. In other countries drops included: [[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-Sexton-9)
*   2% in Canada,  
*   3% in Norway,  
*   6% in West Germany,  
*   7% in Switzerland,  
*   9% in Austria,  
*   14% in the United Kingdom,  
*   15% in Italy.
A CGT banner during a 2005 demonstration in Paris
The General Confederation of Labour (_CGT_) is a national trade union center, the first of the five major French confederations of trade unions. Until the 1990s it was closely linked to the French Communist Party (PCF).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-10)

## Union growth and decline
Labor unions are active in both the public and private sectors. Major concerns include salaries increased to reflect inflation, regulation of public commodities, and a stronger Caja Costarricense del Seguro Social (Costa Rican Social Security Department). Many labor unions are also asking for increased environmental regulation,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-optimism-32) and increased oversight of cooperative banks.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-avala-33) One important issue for Costa Rica unions is passage a new labor law.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-cambios-34) Former president Laura Chinchilla vetoed it, but Solís appears to want the issue passed, as do many members of the Legislative Assembly.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-avala-33)
Economists have explored the linkage between unionization and levels of overall GDP growth and unemployment, especially in light of the high unemployment in Europe since the 1980s and the stagnation in growth rates. On both the theoretical and the empirical sides, experts have not reached any consensus.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-35)

## Violence in labor disputes
[edit]
Between 1877 and 1968, 700 people have been killed in American labor disputes.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-36) In the 1890s, roughly two American workers were killed and 140 injured for every 100,000 strikers. In France, three French workers were injured for every 100,000 strikers. In the 1890s, only 70 French strikers were arrested per 100,000. For the United States, national arrest rates are simply impossible to compile. In Illinois, the arrest rate for the latter half of the 1890s decade was at least 700 per 100,000 strikers, or ten times that of France; in New York for that decade it was at least 400.
Between 1902 and 1904 in America , at least 198 people were killed, 1,966 workers were injured. One worker was killed and 1,009 were injured for every 100,000 strikers.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-38) Between 1877 and 1968, American state and federal troops intervened in labor disputes more than 160 times, almost invariably on behalf of employers.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-Sexton-9) Business was disrupted, usually by strikes, on 22,793 occasions between 1875 and 1900.
Other examples of the violence both by and against U.S. union members in the late 19th and early 20th centuries include the Centralia Massacre, the Great Railroad Strike of 1922, and the Copper Country Strike of 1913-1914

Chunks: 0,1,2
This page is related to the paper How Trade Unions Increase Welfare by Alejandro Donado and Klaus Wälde, published in the Economic Journal 122 No. 563 (2012): 990 – 1009

## The data
The following figure provides an impression of union membership numbers for a selection of OECD countries. The historical data for Australia, Canada, Denmark, Germany, Norway, Sweden and United Kingdom come from Bain and Price (1980), the historical US data is from Freeman (1998), data for Austria, France, Italy and the Netherlands come from Visser (1989). Data as of 1960 is from OECD (2011). For references, please see the paper.
The data is available as historical data only and in the version as used for the above figure. I hope all copyrights are respected by providing the sources.

## Extracting stylized facts
Here is our result of fitting time and time squared plus a post 1959 dummy (to take the switch to OECD data sources into account) to this data. It clearly shows the inverted U shape and the fact that the peak differs across countries with respect to when and how high it is, as stressed in the paper. The exact specification is available as a STATA do file and the results are in a log file. The STATA data file is here.
This figure contains one country more (Netherlands) than in the paper. The only reason is that one country less gives a nicer picture for the paper. Here we keep the Netherlands for completeness sake.

The database on Institutional Characteristics of Trade Unions, Wage Setting, State Intervention and Social Pacts (ICTWSS) was developed by Prof. Jelle Visser at the University of Amsterdam. It was first released in May 2007. In its initial form, the ICTWSS database combined data from various sources and projects with a main focus on trade union in EU and OECD countries, collective bargaining and employment relations in Europe, and social pacts. In 2021, the ICTWSS database was rebranded as the OECD/AIAS ICTWSS database to reflect the joint effort by the OECD and AIAS-HSI to ensure the continuation of the database following Prof. Visser’s retirement. ## Union growth and decline
[edit]
In the mid-1950s, 36% of the United States labor force was unionized. At America's union peak in the 1950s, union membership was lower in the United States than in most comparable countries. By 1989, that figure had dropped to about 16%, the lowest percentage of any developed democracy, except France. Union membership for other developed democracies, in 1986/87 were:[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-wsj-3)
*   95% in Sweden and Denmark.  
*   85% in Finland  
*   Over 60% in Norway and Austria  
*   Over 50% in Australia, Ireland and the United Kingdom.  
*   Over 40% in Italy.  
*   Over 30% in West Germany.
In 1987, United States unionization was 37 points below the average of seventeen countries surveyed, down from 17 points below average in 1970.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-wsj-3) Between 1970 and 1987, union membership declined in only three other countries: Austria, by 3%, Japan, by 7%, and the Netherlands, by 4%. In the United States, union membership had declined by 14%.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-4)

## Union growth and decline
In 2008, 12.4% of U.S. wage and salary workers were union members. 36.8% of public sector workers were union members, but only 7.6% of workers in private sector industries were.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-5) The most unionized sectors of the economy have had the greatest decline in union membership. From 1953 to the late 1980s membership in construction fell from 84% to 22%, manufacturing from 42% to 25%, mining from 65% to 15%, and transportation from 80% to 37%.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-7)
From 1971 to the late 1980s, there was a 10% drop in union membership in the U.S. public sector and a 42% drop in union membership in the U.S. private sector.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-8) For comparison, there was no drop in union membership in the private sector in Sweden. In other countries drops included: [[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-Sexton-9)
*   2% in Canada,  
*   3% in Norway,  
*   6% in West Germany,  
*   7% in Switzerland,  
*   9% in Austria,  
*   14% in the United Kingdom,  
*   15% in Italy.
A CGT banner during a 2005 demonstration in Paris
The General Confederation of Labour (_CGT_) is a national trade union center, the first of the five major French confederations of trade unions. Until the 1990s it was closely linked to the French Communist Party (PCF).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-10)

## Union growth and decline
Labor unions are active in both the public and private sectors. Major concerns include salaries increased to reflect inflation, regulation of public commodities, and a stronger Caja Costarricense del Seguro Social (Costa Rican Social Security Department). Many labor unions are also asking for increased environmental regulation,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-optimism-32) and increased oversight of cooperative banks.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-avala-33) One important issue for Costa Rica unions is passage a new labor law.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-cambios-34) Former president Laura Chinchilla vetoed it, but Solís appears to want the issue passed, as do many members of the Legislative Assembly.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-avala-33)
Economists have explored the linkage between unionization and levels of overall GDP growth and unemployment, especially in light of the high unemployment in Europe since the 1980s and the stagnation in growth rates. On both the theoretical and the empirical sides, experts have not reached any consensus.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-35)

## Violence in labor disputes
[edit]
Between 1877 and 1968, 700 people have been killed in American labor disputes.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-36) In the 1890s, roughly two American workers were killed and 140 injured for every 100,000 strikers. In France, three French workers were injured for every 100,000 strikers. In the 1890s, only 70 French strikers were arrested per 100,000. For the United States, national arrest rates are simply impossible to compile. In Illinois, the arrest rate for the latter half of the 1890s decade was at least 700 per 100,000 strikers, or ten times that of France; in New York for that decade it was at least 400.
Between 1902 and 1904 in America , at least 198 people were killed, 1,966 workers were injured. One worker was killed and 1,009 were injured for every 100,000 strikers.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-38) Between 1877 and 1968, American state and federal troops intervened in labor disputes more than 160 times, almost invariably on behalf of employers.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_comparisons_of_trade_unions#cite_note-Sexton-9) Business was disrupted, usually by strikes, on 22,793 occasions between 1875 and 1900.
Other examples of the violence both by and against U.S. union members in the late 19th and early 20th centuries include the Centralia Massacre, the Great Railroad Strike of 1922, and the Copper Country Strike of 1913-1914

# 1 out of 7 EU employees is a low-wage earner
© A_stockphoto/Shutterstock.com
In 2022, 14.7% of employees in the EU were low-wage earners, against 16.2% in 2018. Low-wage earners are employees earning two-thirds or less of the median gross hourly earnings in the country of work.
The share of low-wage earners was higher among women than men in 2022 (17.1% compared with 12.6%). In 2018 the shares were 18.2% of female and 12.5% of male employees.
Low-wage earners accounted for about a quarter (25.2%) of employees younger than 30. In the older age groups this share was lower: 12.1% among employees aged 30-49, and 13.4% among those older than 50.

The lower the level of a person’s education, the higher the likelihood of being a low-wage earner. In 2022, 27.5% of employees in the EU with a low education level were low-wage earners, compared with 17.5% of employees with a medium level of education and 4.8% of those with a high education level.

# 1 out of 7 EU employees is a low-wage earner
## Highest share of low-wage earners in Bulgaria, lowest in Portugal
The proportion of low-wage earners varied significantly among EU countries in 2022. The highest share was observed in Bulgaria (26.8%), followed by Romania (23.9%), Latvia (23.3%), Greece (21.7%), Estonia (21.2%) and Cyprus (20.0%).
In contrast, less than 10% of employees were low-wage earners in Portugal (1.8%), Sweden (4.1%), Finland (6.5%), Italy (8.8%), Slovenia (9.4%) and France and Denmark (9.7% both).

## Highest share of low-wage earners in food and accommodation services
In 2022, the share of low-wage earners recorded in the EU was highest in accommodation and food service activities (35.1%); followed by administrative and support service activities (32.3%), that includes the persons employed by interim agencies.
The type of contract also plays a role: among employees with an employment contract of limited duration, 27.2% were low-wage earners, compared with 12.6% of those with an indefinite contract.

Title: How are minimum wages set?
